title: Viennese whirls
subtitle: piped butter biscuits sandwiched with jam and buttercream
excerpt: Viennese whirls are piped butter biscuits with a very high fat content that gives them a melt-in-the-mouth texture. You get a sandwiched biscuit with a layer of buttercream and raspberry jam in the centre. The dough must be soft enough to pipe through a star nozzle but firm enough that the rosette holds its shape in the oven.
sourceNotes: Viennese whirls are a British adaptation of the Viennese biscuit tradition, closely related to Vanillekipferl and Spritzgebäck. The sandwiched version with buttercream and jam became a British patisserie staple in the mid-twentieth century.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the unfilled biscuit shells only. Fill after defrosting.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Unfilled shells keep in an airtight tin for 4 days. Fill shortly before serving; the buttercream softens the biscuit if left overnight.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 190 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 175 degrees Celsius. Middle shelf. The biscuits are very pale when they come out; the base should be just starting to colour.

glossaryTerms.definition: Forcing a very soft butter biscuit dough through a piping bag fitted with a large star nozzle to create shaped biscuits. The dough must be genuinely soft to pipe without the bag splitting, but must also hold the ridged shape of the nozzle once piped. Cornflour in the dough reduces the flour's protein content, which keeps the baked biscuit tender rather than firm.

The crumbly, sandy, melt-in-the-mouth quality of biscuits with a high butter-to-flour ratio. In Viennese whirls, the very high butter content (more butter than flour by weight) combined with a small quantity of cornflour gives an unusually delicate texture that dissolves on the tongue.

A smooth filling made by beating softened butter with sifted icing sugar until pale and fluffy. For Viennese whirls, a small amount of vanilla extract is added. The buttercream must be soft enough to spread or pipe without breaking the delicate biscuit shells, but firm enough to hold its shape in the sandwich.

content.text: . The butter must be very soft before you beat it; if it is too cool the dough will not pipe cleanly through the star nozzle. Cornflour is what gives the biscuit its particular crumble. Pipe the rosettes slightly larger than you want the finished biscuit to be, as they shrink a little during baking.

content.text: Preheat the oven to 190 degrees Celsius. Line two baking trays with baking paper.
Beat the very soft butter and sifted icing sugar together with a hand mixer for 3 to 4 minutes until pale and very fluffy. Beat in the vanilla extract.
Sift the plain flour and cornflour together and fold into the butter mixture with a spatula until just combined. The dough should be very soft and smooth; it should drop off a spoon but not be runny.

Transfer the dough to a piping bag fitted with a large open star nozzle. Pipe 24 rosettes onto the prepared trays, each about 4 cm in diameter, leaving 3 cm between them. Pipe them slightly larger than the finished size you want; the biscuits will shrink slightly in the oven.

Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until the edges just begin to turn pale gold and the base is lightly set. The tops will remain very pale. Leave on the trays for 10 minutes before moving to a cooling rack; these biscuits are fragile when warm.

Beat the 100 g of softened butter until smooth. Gradually beat in the sifted icing sugar in two additions, then the vanilla extract. Beat for 2 to 3 minutes until the buttercream is pale and fluffy. Taste and adjust with more icing sugar if needed.

Match the biscuits into pairs. Spread or pipe a small amount of buttercream onto the flat side of one biscuit from each pair. Add a small amount of raspberry jam to the centre of the buttercream, then press the second biscuit on top, flat side down. Press gently; they break apart easily.

attrs.problem: The dough is too stiff to pipe and the bag is splitting
attrs.avoid: Avoid using butter that is not genuinely very soft; it should be almost room temperature and press easily with a fingertip.
attrs.fix: If the dough is too firm, briefly warm the outside of the piping bag with your hands. If the dough is still not piping, take the dough out of the bag and let it warm at room temperature for 5 minutes, then return it to the bag.

attrs.problem: The biscuits spread flat and lose the piped pattern in the oven
attrs.avoid: Avoid using butter that is too warm; very warm butter produces dough that spreads before it sets.
attrs.fix: If spreading is a problem, chill the piped rosettes on the tray for 10 to 15 minutes before baking. This firms the butter so the ridged shape holds in the initial heat of the oven.

attrs.problem: The biscuits break apart when sandwiching
attrs.avoid: Avoid handling the biscuits while they are still warm; they are very fragile until fully cooled.
attrs.fix: Ensure the biscuits are completely cool before filling. Handle them by their edges rather than picking them up from the top or bottom. If a biscuit cracks, it can still be sandwiched; the buttercream holds the halves together.
